title: Representation in First Nations Australian literature

draft.title: Representation in First Nations Australian literature
card: First Nations Australian authors write about their own peoples, Country and histories. They speak from their own experience and knowledge.
Country is a word for the land, waters and sky, and the living connections that First Nations peoples have with them.
Earlier texts about First Nations peoples were often made by others, such as non-Indigenous writers. Those texts could be limited, one-sided or inaccurate.
Many First Nations authors challenge these earlier representations. They offer their own viewpoints, stories and voices instead.
draft.remember: First Nations authors represent their own peoples and Country, and often challenge earlier representations made by others.

a.q: Why do many First Nations authors challenge earlier representations of their peoples?
opts: Earlier texts by others were often limited or one-sided
Earlier texts were always written by First Nations authors
Earlier texts never mentioned First Nations peoples at all
Earlier texts were too long for modern readers
a.why: Many earlier texts were made by others and could be limited or inaccurate, so First Nations authors offer their own viewpoints. The card does not say earlier texts never mentioned First Nations peoples, only that their portrayals could be flawed.
a.clue: Think about who made the earlier texts.

b.q: A First Nations author writes a story about her family's Country that shows its history through her own community's voice. What is she doing?
opts: Representing her own people and Country from within
Describing a place she has only read about in books
Copying an earlier text made by outside writers
Avoiding any connection to history or place
b.why: She writes from her own community's experience, which is how First Nations authors represent their own peoples and Country. It is not an outsider's view, so the option about reading from books is wrong.
b.clue: Who is telling the story, and whose Country is it?

a.best: Earlier texts by others were often limited or one-sided

b.best: Representing her own people and Country from within

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('often'). Two distractors use 'always' and 'never', and one contradicts the question's own premise, so a student can pick the answer by eliminating the absolutes without knowing the idea.

The right option is the only one that echoes the stem's wording ('her own', 'Country'), and the other three plainly contradict the scenario. The answer can be picked by matching words rather than understanding.

check.summary: The content is accurate and fits the point. Both questions are too easy to game: in (a) the right answer is the only hedged option against absolute distractors, and in (b) it is the only one that echoes the stem against obviously wrong alternatives.

proposal.title: Representation in First Nations Australian literature
card: First Nations Australian authors write about their own peoples, Country and histories. They write as insiders, from their own experience and knowledge.
Country is a word for the land, waters and sky, and the living connections that First Nations peoples have with them.
Earlier texts about First Nations peoples were often made by others, such as non-Indigenous writers. Those texts could be limited, one-sided or inaccurate.
Many First Nations authors challenge these earlier representations. They offer their own viewpoints, stories and voices instead.
proposal.remember: Insiders telling their own stories can challenge the way outsiders once portrayed them.

a.q: What makes a First Nations author's representation different from many earlier ones?
opts: It comes from the community being portrayed
It comes from an outside expert who studied the community
It comes from a writer who avoids history and place
It comes from official records kept about the community
a.why: First Nations authors write as insiders about their own peoples, Country and histories. An outside expert is still one of the others who made many earlier texts, so that option describes the older kind of representation.
a.clue: Think about who is doing the telling.

b.q: An old novel by a visiting settler showed Aboriginal people only as silent figures in the background. Today, Leah, a First Nations author, writes a novel in which an Aboriginal family from that region tells its own story. What is Leah's novel doing?
opts: Challenging an outsider's portrayal with an insider's view
Repeating the older portrayal in a more modern style
Giving an outsider's view of a community she visited
Moving the story from that region to an invented place
b.why: The family tells its own story, so Leah offers an insider's view that answers the settler's one-sided picture. It is not an outsider's view, because the voice comes from the community itself.
b.clue: Compare who speaks in each novel.
